newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH Q4 GDP GROWTH STRONG, DIMS HOPE FOR RATE CUT.
newsitem.headline: CZECH Q4 GDP GROWTH STRONG, DIMS HOPE FOR RATE CUT.

text.p: The Czech economy grew faster than expected in the fourth quarter of 1996, dimming hopes that the central bank will move in the near future to cut interest rates.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) on Friday released figures showing fourth quarter GDP growth was a surprisingly robust 4.7 percent, year-on-year, more than one percentage point higher than a Reuters survey of economists predicted.

The strong fourth quarter performance, and an upward revision of second quarter GDP to 4.6 percent from a previous 4.0 percent, helped push full year 1996 GDP to 4.4 percent, 80 basis points points higher than forecast in the Reuters survey.
Analysts said that with the central bank's fight against inflation still the focus of its policies, the strong growth figures should remove any room for a change in interest rates.
"For the currency markets it means the crown may not weaken...it means the central bank is less likely to cut rates," John Vax director of capital markets at ING Barings in Prague told Reuters.

Last summer, the central bank hiked its key discount rate by one full percentage point to 10.5 percent, and implemented a series of measures incluing repo rate hikes and raising minimum reserve requirements to choke a burgeoning money supply and ease inflationary pressures.

The moves appear to be working, with the M2 money supply, which measures currency, demand deposits, time and savings deposits, and foreign currency deposits, easing to 7.8 percent in December from 20.2 percent in the same month of 1995.
In addition, inflation has continued its gradual easing, dipping to 7.3 percent year-on-year in February.
But Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus recently complained that the central bank measures had gone too far, and that a relaxation of monetary policy was needed.

Kamil Janacek, chief economist at Komercni Banka, said that the upturn in the final quarter of last year, was partly due to the weakness of the last quarter of 1995 -- the base against which the new figure was calculated.
"The fourth quarter of 1995 was rather poor so also a statistical factor is playing some role," Janacek said.

The Czech economy has enjoyed seven years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and the population, which has seen its wages rise sharply over the past few years, slaked its thirst for consumer goods.

However, some economists say that cracks have begun to appear with industrial output failing to keep pace with wages, and in fact weakening recently, indicating that investment has not been effective and that industry has not carried out vital restructuring.

Last week, the CSU released figures showing real industrial output contracted by 3.9 percent year-on-year in January and that construction output was 18.6 percent lower than a year earlier. At the same time, average industrial wages grew 14.4 percent in nominal terms.

Zdenek Tuma, chief economist at Patria Finance investment bank agreed that the GDP figures were better than expected but said the markets would have to weigh up the relative importance of 1996 GDP against the poor 1997 numbers released so far this year.

"There were bad figures at the beginning of the year so the question is whether the results for the whole of 1996 will be perceived as more important than the figures at the beginning of 1997," he said.
